Apple root rot: causes, signs and what to do

Apple root rot is caused by soil fungi that attack roots in wet, poorly drained soil. Trees show weak growth, yellow leaves and small fruit, then die over one or two seasons. Better drainage, healthy soil and early action lower the losses.
problem-apple-root-rot.webp
Clear field photo showing apple root rot
Leaves turn pale or yellow and fall early.
New shoots are short; the tree looks tired.
Fruit is small and colours poorly.
Bark at the collar (soil level) is dark, soft or cracked.
Roots are brown and soft instead of white and firm.
Why it happens
Water standing around the trunk after rain or irrigation.
Heavy soil with little air.
Old orchard soil with few helpful soil organisms left.
Wounds on roots and collar from tools or pests.
Trees already weak from heavy cropping or stress.
What growers can do
Make sure water drains away from trunks; open drains in low spots.
Keep the collar clear of soil, mulch and weeds.
Avoid wounding roots and the collar.
Build soil organic matter so helpful organisms return.
Get badly affected trees checked by an expert; follow their advice on treatment.
Remove dead trees and roots before replanting.
See the full apple guide and Immunity Apple Special.
Can a tree with root rot recover?
Trees caught early, with part of the root system still healthy, can recover if drainage and soil are fixed. Trees with most roots gone rarely do.
Is root rot the same as collar rot?
They are related. Collar rot attacks the trunk at soil level, root rot attacks the roots. Both are favoured by wet soil.
Where does Immunity Apple Special fit?
It supports roots and soil life as part of orchard care. It is not a fungicide; disease control follows an expert's advice.

Citrus dieback: why branches dry from the tip

Citrus dieback, where branches dry from the tip back, has several causes: root rot from poor drainage, nutrient shortages such as zinc, pests and old age. Fixing the root zone and nutrition comes before pruning dry branches.
problem-citrus-dieback.webp
Clear field photo showing citrus dieback
Common causes
Root rot and gummosis in wet soil.
Zinc, iron and other micronutrient shortage, especially in alkaline soil.
Pests such as bark borers.
Old, neglected trees.
Improve drainage; keep water off the trunk.
Test soil and leaves for nutrient shortage.
Prune dead wood back to healthy tissue.
Feed the tree and build soil organic matter.
See the full citrus guide and Immunity Citrus Special.
Should I cut the dry branches?
Yes, prune back to healthy wood, but also find the cause, or the dieback will return.

Mango alternate bearing: why trees fruit every other year

A mango tree that carries a heavy crop uses up its stored food and makes little new growth, so it flowers poorly the next year. Feeding after harvest, timely pruning and steady nutrition help the tree make new shoots every year.
problem-mango-alternate-bearing.webp
Clear field photo showing mango alternate bearing
How the cycle works
Fruit grows on shoots that matured in the season before.
A heavy crop takes the food that would have built new shoots.
Few mature shoots means few flowers next year, and the cycle repeats.
Harvest on time and prune soon after harvest to start new growth.
Feed the tree after harvest, when it is building next year's shoots.
Thin very heavy crops on young trees.
Keep records of each tree's yield to see the pattern.
See the full mango guide and Immunity Mango Special.
Are some mango varieties more prone to alternate bearing?
Yes. Many traditional varieties bear alternately more than some newer ones.
Can alternate bearing be stopped completely?
It can be reduced, not always removed. Good care over several seasons evens out the crop.

Some fruit drop in mango is natural: a tree sets far more fruit than it can carry. Heavy drop follows stress, such as dry soil, hot winds, pests like hoppers, or a tree low on stored food. Steady water and nutrition through fruit set reduce it.
problem-mango-fruit-drop.webp
Clear field photo showing mango flower and fruit drop
Natural drop and problem drop
A mango panicle carries hundreds of flowers but keeps only a few fruits; most of the drop in the first weeks is normal.
Problem drop is when most young fruit falls, or fruit keeps falling at marble size and later.
Dry soil during fruit set and growth.
Hot, dry winds.
Hoppers, mealybugs and other pests on the panicles.
Poor pollination in cloudy or rainy weather.
A tree weak from a heavy crop last year.
Keep soil moisture steady from fruit set onward; avoid sudden heavy watering after a dry spell.
Watch panicles for hoppers and act early.
Feed the tree after harvest so it has reserves for next season.
Mulch the basin to hold moisture.
When should I water mango trees during fruiting?
Once fruit has set, light and regular watering is better than none or very heavy watering. Your local horticulture office can advise for your soil.
Does alternate bearing cause fruit drop?
In the off year the tree has fewer reserves, so it holds less fruit. Good care after harvest helps both problems.

Potato fertilizer schedule: stage-by-stage nutrition plan

A good potato fertilizer schedule follows the crop: organic manure and the basal dose before planting, the rest of the nitrogen at earthing up, steady water and potash through tuber initiation and bulking, and no irrigation in the last 10 to 15 days. The exact amounts should come from your soil test.
potato-schedule-field-stages.webp
Photo of a potato field at earthing up, with ridges and healthy green plants
Before planting
Get a soil test; it decides how much nitrogen, phosphorus and potash your field needs.
Mix well-rotted farmyard manure or compost into the field.
Apply the full phosphorus and potash and about half of the nitrogen as the basal dose at planting, unless your soil test advice says otherwise.
Biofertilizers such as Azotobacter and PSB can go in with the manure.
Earthing up (about 25 to 30 days after planting)
Apply the remaining nitrogen just before earthing up.
Earth up well so tubers stay covered and protected.
Irrigate lightly after earthing up.
Tuber initiation (about 35 to 50 days)
This is when the plant decides how many tubers it will carry; avoid any water stress.
Correct zinc or boron shortage if your soil test shows it.
Biostimulants and crop formulas such as Immunity Potato Special are used around this stage to support roots.
Bulking (about 50 to 80 days)
Tubers grow in size and weight; potash and steady water matter most.
Protect the leaves from late blight; healthy leaves fill the tubers.
Avoid late nitrogen; it delays maturity and weakens skins.
Maturity and harvest
Stop irrigation about 10 to 15 days before harvest.
Cut haulms when advised so the skin sets.
Harvest when skins do not peel when rubbed.
When should urea be applied to potato?
A common practice is half the nitrogen at planting and the rest at earthing up, about 25 to 30 days after planting. Follow your soil test advice for the amount.
When should I stop irrigating potato before harvest?
About 10 to 15 days before harvest, so the skins set and the tubers store well.

Soil fertility: nutrients, organic carbon and soil tests

Soil fertility is the soil's ability to supply the nutrients a crop needs, in the right amounts and at the right time. It depends on the nutrients present, on organic carbon and pH, and on the soil organisms that make nutrients available.
soil-test-report-farmer.webp
Photo of a farmer holding a soil health card or soil test report in the field
Nutrients crops need
Major: nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K)
Secondary: calcium, magnesium, sulphur
Micronutrients: zinc, iron, boron, manganese, copper, molybdenum
Why organic carbon matters
Organic carbon is the best single sign of soil fertility. It holds nutrients and water, feeds soil organisms and keeps the soil crumbly. Many Indian soils now test low in organic carbon.
Why pH matters
Most nutrients are easiest for plants to take up in near-neutral soil
In alkaline soil, zinc, iron and phosphorus get locked up
In acidic soil, phosphorus and some micronutrients get locked up
Locked nutrients

Soil often holds plenty of phosphorus, potash and zinc that the crop cannot use. Phosphate-solubilising, potash-mobilising and zinc-solubilising bacteria help release them, which is why our biofertilizer range includes PSB, KMB and ZSB.
How often should I test my soil?
Every two to three years for each field, and whenever yields drop without a clear reason.
What is a good organic carbon level?
Soil labs commonly treat below about 0.5 percent as low. Ask your lab for the local standard.

Sustainable farming and the 5 Rs

Sustainable farming means growing good crops at a fair cost without using up the soil, water and health the next generation will need. The 5 Rs (reduce, reuse, recycle, restore and restrict) are a simple way to put it into practice.
sustainable-farm-wide.webp
Wide photo of a green, mulched farm with compost heap and healthy crop, farmer walking in the field
Reduce
Use fertilizer and chemicals based on need, not habit. A soil test and a crop schedule usually show where money is being wasted.
Reuse
Return crop residue to the soil as mulch instead of burning it. Residue is free organic matter.
Recycle
Turn farm waste, dung and residue into compost. Good compost is the cheapest soil improver a farmer can make.
Restore
Bring soil life back with organic matter, biofertilizers and biostimulants. Living soil feeds the crop better.
Restrict
Limit hazardous chemicals that kill soil life, pollute water and leave residues in food. Use them only when truly needed, and safely.
Our part
Our mission is to make farming free of hazardous chemicals and make sustainable food growing easier for the generations to come. Every Immunity formula is made with that aim.
Does sustainable farming mean lower yields?
Not necessarily. Many growers keep yields while cutting costs once the soil recovers; results vary by farm.
Where should a farmer start?
With a soil test and compost. Those two steps show what the soil needs and start rebuilding it.

Calcium travels in the plant only with the water stream to the leaves. Fruits lose little water, so they get little calcium, and any break in water supply cuts it further. Too much potash, magnesium or ammonium also crowds calcium out, and without boron calcium cannot do its job in the cell wall. That is why a field can show calcium problems on calcium-rich soil, and why calcium sprays alone often fail.
The real causes
Irregular watering: the biggest cause of blossom-end rot.
Humid, still weather that slows water movement.
Heavy potash, magnesium or ammonium nitrogen.
Boron shortage, which stops calcium from building cell walls.
Very fast growth from heavy nitrogen.
What fixes it
Water little and often during fruit growth.
Balance potash and nitrogen to the soil test.
Check magnesium and boron along with calcium.
Use calcium sprays at fruit development as a support, not the only fix.

What happens when micronutrients are not managed

A micronutrient shortage limits the whole crop, however much NPK is applied. It shows as weak germination and growth, poor flowering and fruit set, fruit drop, small and low-quality produce with low brix and poor shelf life, and lower market prices. It also wastes fertilizer and leaves the crop weaker against pests, diseases, heat, cold, drought and salt.

The law of the minimum

A crop grows only as well as its scarcest nutrient allows. Think of a bucket made of wooden staves of different heights: water fills only up to the shortest stave. If zinc or boron is the short stave, more urea or DAP raises the other staves but not the water level. This is why yields can stay flat while fertilizer bills rise.
Hidden hunger

Yield is often lost before any symptom appears. A crop slightly short of a micronutrient looks normal but grows and yields less. Soil surveys count these latent shortages too. By the time leaves show it, a part of the yield is already gone, so testing before the season is worth more than spraying after symptoms appear.

Unused nitrogen washes out or escapes to the air, wasting money and harming water and soil.
Rising doses without rising yields are a common sign of a hidden micronutrient limit.
More pest and disease problems
Crops short of zinc, manganese, copper, boron, calcium and silicon have weaker cell walls and defences.
Soft, lush growth from heavy nitrogen with poor balance attracts sucking pests.
Sprays then rise, adding cost and residue. Balanced nutrition is part of pest and disease prevention, not a replacement for scouting and control.

Silicon and potassium help crops hold water and stand up.
A well-fed crop recovers faster after stress.
For people and animals
Grain grown on zinc and iron-poor soil carries less zinc and iron for the people who eat it, and fodder poor in cobalt, copper or selenium affects animal health. Healthy soil grows healthier food.

Yes. This hidden hunger cuts yield before any leaf symptom appears. Soil testing before the season finds it.

Does good nutrition reduce pests and diseases?
Balanced nutrition makes crops harder to attack and quicker to recover, but it does not replace scouting and pest control.

Fields that received some industrial wastes or sludge.
The top few centimetres of soil, where it does not move down.
How to keep it in balance

Follow the disease forecast and label instead of calendar spraying.
Add organic matter to support soil life.
Do not add copper fertilizer where tests show enough.

Silicon in rice and sugarcane: stronger stems and fewer pest and disease problems

Rice and sugarcane take up more silicon than almost any other nutrient. They lay it down in their leaves and stems, which become stronger, stand more upright and resist stem borers, planthoppers and fungal diseases. When straw, husk and trash are burnt or carried away, that silicon leaves the field. Returning residues and using silicate sources keeps it in balance.
What silicon does in these crops
Stiffer stems, less lodging.
Upright leaves that catch more light.
Harder tissue against borers and planthoppers.
Less blast and brown spot in rice.
Better tolerance to drought and salt.
Keeping silicon in the field
Do not burn straw or trash; incorporate or compost it.
Use rice husk and husk ash where available.
Use silicate sources or soluble silicon sprays as advised.

Does burning sugarcane trash remove silicon?
Burning or carrying away trash and straw removes the silicon they hold from the field and damages soil organic matter.
Will silicon replace pesticides?
No. It strengthens the crop's own defences, which can reduce pest and disease pressure. Pest control still follows field scouting.

Zinc and phosphorus: why heavy DAP can cause zinc deficiency

Phosphorus and zinc compete. When a field gets heavy phosphate year after year, the crop can take up less zinc, and the soil's zinc becomes less available, especially in alkaline soils. The answer is not less phosphorus where the crop needs it, but balanced feeding: phosphorus by soil test, and zinc applied where the test shows it is short.
Signs in a DAP-heavy field
High phosphate in the soil can bind zinc into forms roots cannot use.
Inside the plant, very high phosphorus can reduce the zinc that reaches new leaves.
Alkaline, calcareous soils make the problem worse.
Signs in a DAP-heavy field
Good early colour but small, narrow new leaves.
Patchy growth even with plenty of NPK.
Yields that stopped rising though fertilizer use keeps rising.
Test the soil and apply phosphorus to the test, not by habit.
Apply zinc separately from phosphate fertilizers, not mixed in the same bag.
Use foliar zinc on the standing crop if new growth shows shortage.
Build organic matter, which keeps both phosphorus and zinc available.

Zinc deficiency symptoms crop by crop

Zinc deficiency looks different in each crop, but the common thread is the young growth: small, narrow, pale leaves, short internodes and stunted plants. In paddy it shows as rusty brown spots after transplanting, in maize as a pale band beside the midrib, and in citrus as yellow mottling with small pointed leaves.

Pale stripes on young leaves, short internodes and poor tillering in calcareous soils.
Narrow, pointed, pale young leaves, sometimes with a reddish tinge underneath.
Little leaf and rosetting of new flushes, weak flowering.

Iron shortage also yellows young leaves, but the leaf keeps its normal size.
Leaf curl virus and sucking pests also make small, curled young leaves; check the leaf underside for insects.
Herbicide drift distorts leaves suddenly over a patch or along the field edge.
Waterlogging and cold weather cause general paleness that clears when the weather does.
